The foundational tension between risk, uncertainty, and profit reflects the core challenge of modeling complex systems. Analytical methods, while powerful, are inherently incomplete due to the exponential growth of degrees of freedom in real-world scenarios. This limitation necessitates reliance on dominant element approximations—whereby only a few critical variables govern behavior. These elements form the kernel of predictive models, enabling approximate yet useful insights. However, this approach fails when variability or rare events disrupt the dominance of key factors. The mathematical structure underlying this framework involves probabilistic reasoning, where risk is quantified through variance, uncertainty through entropy, and profit through expected returns adjusted for risk. In GSI, these concepts map directly to Bayesian updating and conformal prediction. In GSE, they inform state-transition logic based on dominant causal structures rather than exhaustive enumeration.
